questions.learningObjective: invert the power rule to find an antiderivative of a fractional power
questions.stem: An antiderivative of the function whose value at x is the square root of x must differentiate back to the square root of x. Which candidate does that?

options.text: the fraction 2 over 3 times x to the power 3 over 2, whose derivative is the square root of x by the reverse power rule
the quantity x to the power 3 over 2 on its own, whose derivative is 3 over 2 times the square root of x, not the square root of x
options.misconception: applies the reverse power rule but forgets the division by the new exponent three over two

options.text: the quantity x squared over 2, whose derivative is x, a different function from the square root of x entirely
options.misconception: reads the index two of the square root as the exponent two and integrates a square

options.text: the quantity 1 over the quantity 2 x squared, whose derivative is minus 1 over x cubed, a reciprocal rather than a root
options.misconception: halves the exponent when undoing a square root instead of adding one to it

questions.explanation: The reverse power rule says the antiderivative of x to the n is x to the n plus 1 divided by n plus 1, valid whenever n is not minus 1. Differentiating that confirms it, since two thirds times three halves is exactly 1, which cancels the three halves and leaves x to the one half, the square root of x. Option B keeps the right shape but drops the factor, so it differentiates to three halves of a root. Option D comes from halving the exponent, and halving gives a negative power whose derivative lands on a reciprocal.

At 3 that is 2 times 27, or 54; at 1 it is 2 times 1, or 2; the difference is 54 minus 2, which is 52. A second route confirms it: let u equal x cubed, so that 6 x squared dx becomes 2 du, and the bounds x = 1 and x = 3 become u = 1 and u = 27, giving 2 times 27 minus 1, again 52. The two routes agree, which is the check that the constant was folded in correctly.
questions.hint: The antiderivative is 2 x cubed; subtract its value at the lower limit from its value at the upper one.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: state the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and identify both halves
questions.stem: Suppose F of x is an antiderivative of a function f of x that is continuous on a closed interval. What does the definite integral of f from a to b equal?

options.text: F of b minus F of a, so the net change in the antiderivative carries the signed area under the curve
F of a minus F of b, because a definite integral is written with the left endpoint acting first
options.misconception: reverses the endpoint order, which is the rule for a reversed limit of integration

options.text: F of b plus F of a, because a definite integral accumulates a value at each endpoint and adds them
options.misconception: adds the two endpoint values, as though the integral were a sum of two evaluations

options.text: the average of F of a and F of b, because every integral of this shape produces a mean value
options.misconception: confuses the average-value formula for f with a difference of endpoint values

questions.explanation: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus has two halves that answer two different questions. The first half says that when f is continuous and F is any antiderivative of it, the definite integral of f from a to b is F of b minus F of a, so accumulation of a rate over an interval is measured as a net change in a quantity whose rate it is. The second half runs the other way: if the integrand is continuous, then differentiating the definite integral of f with respect to its upper limit returns f itself. The direction of the subtraction in the first half is fixed by the limit convention, since reversing the limits negates the integral.
questions.hint: Accumulation is a net change, and a net change is an ending value minus a starting value.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: distinguish total distance travelled from net change in position
questions.stem: A car moves along a straight road with signed velocity v of t = t squared minus 4, and the record runs from t = 0 to t = 3. Explain why the total distance it covers and its net change in position are different numbers here, showing the splitting argument.

answer.exemplar: A definite integral of a signed velocity adds positive motion to negative motion, so any segment where the velocity is negative cancels part of the total. Solving t squared minus 4 equal to 0 gives t = 2, and the velocity is negative on the interval from 0 to 2 and positive on the interval from 2 to 3, so the cancellation happens in the first window. The net change in position is the single definite integral of t squared minus 4 from 0 to 3, whose antiderivative is t cubed over 3 minus 4 t; at 3 that is 9 minus 12, or minus 3, at 0 it is 0, so the net change is minus 3 units, meaning the car finishes 3 units behind where it started. The total distance is different because it must be built from the magnitude of the velocity, so the interval is split at t = 2 and each piece is taken positively. The piece from 0 to 2 has integral 8 over 3 minus 8, which is minus 16 over 3, contributing 16 over 3 units of distance. The piece from 2 to 3 has integral 9 minus 8 over 3 minus the piece below 2, which is 7 over 3, contributing 7 over 3 units. The total distance is 16 over 3 plus 7 over 3, which is 23 over 3 units, while the two signed pieces sum to minus 16 over 3 plus 7 over 3, which is minus 3, matching the net change exactly. The gap between 23 over 3 and 3 is the evidence of the cancellation: the car travels a long way backwards at the start and only partly recovers at the end, so the odometer reading and the map position disagree.

questions.explanation: The signed integral of a velocity measures displacement, and it can be negative or smaller than the distance because pieces in opposite directions subtract. The root of the expression t squared minus 4 is t = 2, and that single point splits the interval into a stretch of negative velocity and a stretch of positive velocity. Distance has to be assembled from the absolute value on each stretch, whereas displacement comes from one integral across the whole interval. The two computations below differ by exactly the amount of the backward travel, which is the cancellation made visible.
questions.hint: Find where the velocity changes sign, then compare one integral across the whole interval with two integrals taken positively.

questions.learningObjective: state the convergence condition for an improper integral at infinity
questions.stem: What has to be examined before the improper integral of 1 over x squared from 1 to infinity can be declared convergent?

options.text: whether the antiderivative evaluated at a large cutoff has a finite limit, since only the tail can fail to settle
whether the integrand stays continuous at every point of the closed interval, since any break ruins the integral
options.misconception: insists on continuity on a closed interval, which is irrelevant to a limit at infinity

options.text: whether the integral can be written in closed form without a calculator, before convergence is claimed
options.misconception: confuses the absence of an elementary antiderivative with divergence

options.text: whether the antiderivative stays nonnegative for all large x, since a negative tail cannot be an area

questions.explanation: An improper integral has no endpoint to evaluate at, so it is defined as a limit: the integral from 1 to infinity of 1 over x squared is the limit as b grows without bound of the integral from 1 to b. Convergence is exactly the question of whether that limit is finite. Here the antiderivative is minus 1 over x, so the truncated integral is minus 1 over b plus 1, and as b grows the term minus 1 over b tends to 0, leaving 1. The comparison test generalises the answer: a tail behaving like 1 over x to the p converges exactly when p is greater than 1, and at p = 1 the truncated value is the natural logarithm of b, which has no finite limit.
questions.hint: Replace infinity by a cutoff b and ask whether the truncated value approaches a finite number as b grows.

As b grows, b to the minus 2 tends to 0, so the limit is one half. A shortcut confirms it: for an integral from 1 to infinity of 1 over x to the p, the value is 1 over p minus 1 whenever p is greater than 1, and with p = 3 that is 1 over 2. questions.learningObjective: justify the sign convention for reversed limits of integration
questions.stem: The rule that reversing the limits negates a definite integral is sometimes taken on faith. What actually forces it?

options.text: additivity does: the integral from a to c splits into a to b plus b to c, so the b to a part must be the negative of a to b
the antiderivative happens to be evaluated from right to left, which is a consequence of the notation
options.misconception: believes the sign comes from an order of arithmetic evaluation rather than from orientation

options.text: a convention that subtracts any negative integral from zero before reporting it
options.misconception: invents a subtraction rule for negative integrals that the definition does not contain

options.text: the fundamental theorem is only ever stated with the limits written in decreasing order
options.misconception: misremembers the theorem as requiring decreasing limits, which would change nothing

questions.explanation: The sign is a consequence of additivity, not a convention. Suppose the integral is additive over adjacent intervals, so the integral from a to c equals the integral from a to b plus the integral from b to c for any b between a and c. Now let b tend to a: the first piece on the right has a vanishing interval and tends to zero, leaving the integral from a to c equal to the integral from a to c trivially, but the informative case is taking c to a. Then additivity reads the integral from a to a, which is zero, as the integral from a to b plus the integral from b to a, forcing the integral from b to a to be the negative of the integral from a to b. Orientation is the whole content: a region swept backwards accumulates negatively.
questions.hint: Set one of the three additivity points equal to another and see what the remaining piece must be.

because a reciprocal is never differentiable, so no calculus operation at all can be applied to it
options.misconception: believes reciprocals admit no derivative, ignoring that 1 over x has derivative minus 1 over x squared

options.text: because the exponent minus 1 makes the antiderivative grow without bound as x approaches 0
options.misconception: confuses a blow-up at a boundary with a failure of antiderivatives to exist

options.text: because logarithms are only required when the exponent is larger than 1, which is the opposite of the case that produces them

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: state both halves of the fundamental theorem in rate and total language
questions.practice: explaining the theorem as a rate-total link
questions.stem: Describe the fundamental theorem of calculus as a single idea about rates and totals, stating what each of its two halves says about a quantity and the rate at which it changes.

answer.exemplar: The unifying idea is that a rate and a total are two descriptions of the same information seen from opposite ends, and the theorem says the two ends match up exactly. Fix a continuous function f and call it the rate of change of an unknown quantity S. The first half says the total change in S over the interval from a to b is the definite integral of f from a to b, that is the accumulated area under the rate curve, with sign. Since that total change must also be the difference S of b minus S of a, and an antiderivative F of f satisfies the same rate, the accumulated area is forced to be F of b minus F of a. That is the direction that makes integration useful for computation: find an antiderivative in closed form and subtract. The second half runs the same match-up the other way and is the one that is surprising. It says that if you define a function by accumulating from a fixed start, namely G of x equals the integral of f from a to x, then G grows at exactly the rate f at every point, because the extra sliver of area between x and x plus a small increment h is approximately f of x times h, and dividing by h and taking the limit returns f of x. In symbols the derivative with respect to x of the integral of f of t from a to x equals f of x. The two halves are converses in spirit: one passes from a rate to a total, the other from a total back to a rate, and that they are genuine inverses is the content of the theorem. The honest limitation is the continuity hypothesis, because a jump in f leaves a definite integral undefined and would make the accumulated function have corners, so the derivative in the second half would not exist at the jump.

questions.explanation: Both halves of the theorem connect the same pair of objects, a rate of change and an accumulated total, and the pair of statements are converses: one says a total is recoverable from a rate by integration, the other says a rate is recoverable from a total by differentiation. Writing the accumulation as a function of its upper limit makes the second half fall out of a small-increment argument, since the extra area over a short interval is approximately the rate times the length of that interval. The continuity hypothesis is what makes both halves legitimate, since a jump leaves a definite integral undefined.
questions.hint: Frame it as one question asked twice: how do a total and its rate determine each other?

options.text: the change in litres equals the mean of the starting and ending amounts multiplied by the elapsed time
options.misconception: confuses a change in the amount with a linear interpolation of the amounts

The rate has units of litres per hour, and integrating with respect to a time measured in hours multiplies by hours, so the hours cancel and what remains is litres, which is exactly the unit of a change in the amount. That is not a coincidence: it is the general reason a definite integral of a rate is a total. The other options each fail the unit test in a way that is diagnostic. Integrating the amount itself would give litres times hours, a different physical quantity. Multiplying the endpoint rate by the whole interval is dimensionally fine but silently assumes the rate never changes. Averaging the two amounts is dimensionally wrong as well, since it multiplies an amount by a time.
questions.hint: Do the unit arithmetic: per-hour times hours must come out as the unit of the thing being accumulated.

questions.learningObjective: write the decomposition for a repeated linear factor
questions.stem: The rational function with numerator 3 x and denominator the quantity x minus 2 all squared is to be decomposed. What is the correct form?

questions.stem: A right triangle has vertices at (0,0), (3,0) and (3,3), with all lengths in centimetres, and it is rotated about the y-axis. What is the exact volume of the solid in cubic centimetres?

options.text: 18 pi cubic centimetres, from 2 pi times the integral of x squared from 0 to 3
27 pi cubic centimetres, which is the full cylinder of radius 3 and height 3 with nothing removed
options.misconception: keeps the entire cylinder and overlooks the cone-shaped void that sits near the axis

options.text: 9 pi cubic centimetres, which is pi times the integral of x squared, as though the axis were the x-axis
options.misconception: sets up a disc integral about the x-axis while the rotation is about the y-axis

options.text: 36 pi cubic centimetres, which is the shell result counted once for each side of the axis of rotation
options.misconception: counts the swept region twice, as though material lay on both sides of the axis

questions.explanation: By shells, a strip at radius x has circumference 2 pi x and height x, so the volume is 2 pi times the integral of x squared from 0 to 3, which is 2 pi times the quantity x cubed over 3 at 3, that is 2 pi times 9, which is 18 pi. Seeing the solid gives the same answer independently: the rotated triangle is a cylinder of radius 3 and height 3 with a cone of radius 3 and height 3 removed, the cylinder being 27 pi and the cone being one third of pi times 9 times 3, which is 9 pi, leaving 18 pi. Washers about the y-axis agree as well, since at height y the cross-section runs from radius y out to radius 3, and the integral of pi of 9 minus y squared from 0 to 3 is again 18 pi.
questions.hint: Name the solid first: a cylinder about the y-axis minus the cone cut out by the sloping edge.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: confirm a volume by computing it two independent ways
questions.stem: The region bounded by y = x squared, the line y = 4, and the line x = 0 is rotated about the y-axis. Which value is the volume of the resulting solid?

options.text: 8 pi cubic units, which both the shell method and the washer method produce for this one solid
16 pi cubic units, which is the shell answer doubled on the assumption that the region is symmetric
options.misconception: doubles the volume on the assumption that the region mirrors itself across the axis of rotation

options.text: 16 over 3 pi cubic units, which is the disc integral about the x-axis rather than the y-axis
options.misconception: sets up a disc integral about the x-axis while claiming a rotation about the y-axis

options.text: 32 over 3 pi cubic units, which is the shell integral with the radius left out of the integrand
options.misconception: omits the radius from the shell formula, which already supplies it as the variable of integration

questions.explanation: The shells method integrates 2 pi times x times the height of 4 minus x squared from 0 to 2, and the antiderivative is 2 x squared minus x to the fourth over 4, which is 8 minus 4, that is 4, so the volume is 8 pi. The washers method says the cross-section at height y runs from radius the square root of y out to radius 2, so the volume is pi times the integral of 4 minus y from 0 to 4, which is pi times the quantity 4 y minus y squared over 2 at 4, that is pi times 8, again 8 pi. Two slicings that disagree would mean one of the setups was wrong, so the agreement is itself the evidence. The distractors correspond to real slips: option C is the integral for rotation about the wrong axis, and option D drops the radius from a formula that already contains it.
questions.hint: Compute it twice, once with shells and once with washers; matching results confirm both setups.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: decide convergence of an improper integral at a finite pole by testing the size of the blow-up
questions.stem: The integral of 1 over x squared from 0 to 1 is improper because the integrand blows up at the left endpoint. What decides its fate here, and what is the outcome?

options.text: it depends on whether the truncated integral has a finite limit as the cutoff approaches 0, and here it does not, so it diverges
it converges, because the exponent 2 exceeds 1 and the test for tails at infinity therefore settles it
options.misconception: borrows the convergence test for a tail at infinity and applies it to a pole at a finite endpoint

options.text: it diverges, because any integrand with a pole inside the interval is automatically divergent
options.misconception: treats every pole as automatically divergent, without testing how fast the integrand grows

options.text: it converges conditionally, because the region beyond the pole cancels the region before it
options.misconception: invents a region past the pole to cancel, although the interval stops at 1

questions.explanation: Convergence at a pole is decided by a limit, and the limit here fails. Replacing the left endpoint with a small positive cutoff gives the integral of x to the power minus 2 from the cutoff to 1, whose antiderivative is minus 1 over x, so the truncated value is 1 over the cutoff minus 1. As the cutoff shrinks towards 0 that quantity grows without bound, so the improper integral diverges. What decides the outcome is the exponent, not the mere presence of a pole: the integral of x to the power minus one half from 0 to 1 converges to 2, because the blow-up there is gentle enough. The distinction is that a power of 1 over x with an exponent of exactly 1 or worse is too slow a decay, and no cancellation can rescue it here since the interval has no second piece.
questions.hint: Cut the pole off with a small positive epsilon and see whether the truncated value stays bounded as epsilon shrinks.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: argue the sign of a definite integral of a positive function from rectangles
questions.stem: A student says the definite integral of a positive continuous function over an interval of positive length must be positive, and asks you to justify it. Give the argument, and say exactly what would have to be false for the claim to fail.

answer.exemplar: The cleanest argument is a rectangle argument. Let the interval from a to b have positive length, and let m be the smallest value the continuous function f takes on that interval, which exists because f is continuous on a closed set and so attains a minimum. Since f is positive, m is positive too. For every x in the interval, f of x is at least m, so the region under the curve from a to b contains a rectangle of height m and width b minus a, and also lies inside a rectangle of height M, the maximum value of f, with the same width. The area of the region is squeezed between m of b minus a and M of b minus a, both of which are positive because m, b minus a and M are all positive. A definite integral is exactly the area of that region when f does not change sign, so the integral is positive, indeed strictly positive. The hypothesis that carries the weight is positivity of the function, and the claim fails the moment that is given up. If f changes sign, so that part of the region lies below the axis, the integral measures signed area and cancellation can drive the total to zero, or even negative, even though the function is nonzero and continuous. The width condition matters as well: on a degenerate interval of length zero the integral is zero no matter how positive the function is, which is why the interval is required to have positive length. Continuity is doing real work in this argument, since without it the minimum m need not be attained and the squeeze cannot be set up, and a function with a downward jump can have a negative integral even while taking only positive values on each side of the jump.

questions.explanation: A definite integral of a nonnegative function is an area, and an area cannot be negative, but that argument needs the extra step of showing the area is not zero either. Continuity on a closed interval guarantees an attained positive minimum, which supplies a rectangle of strictly positive area inside the region. The claim fails if the function takes negative values somewhere, because the integral is then signed and cancellation is possible, and it also fails on a degenerate interval where the width is zero.
questions.hint: Continuity on a closed interval gives an attained minimum; use it to sandwich the region between two rectangles.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: correct a misapplied reverse power rule after a substitution
questions.stem: A student integrates 2 x times the square root of 1 plus x squared from 0 to 3 by setting u = 1 plus x squared, and reports the quantity 10 cubed minus 1 all over 3, which is 333. What is the error, and what is the correct value?

options.text: the power rule was misapplied to the square root, whose antiderivative is two thirds of u to the three halves, so the value is about 20.415184
the substitution was invalid, because u may not be set equal to 1 plus x squared when a square root is present
options.misconception: believes a square root inside the integrand forbids the substitution that the differential calls for

options.text: the limits were wrong, since u at x = 3 is 9 rather than 10, giving a value of about 18
options.misconception: miscounts the transformed limit as 9, forgetting that x squared at 3 is 9 and one more makes 10

options.text: the answer is correct, since 10 cubed minus 1 all over 3 is what the transformed integral evaluates to
options.misconception: accepts a result produced by integrating the wrong power of the new variable

questions.explanation: The substitution is right: du equals 2 x dx, so the integral becomes the integral of the square root of u from u = 1 to u = 10, and the transformed limits are correct because 1 plus 3 squared is 10. The error is in integrating the square root. The reverse power rule adds one to the exponent and divides by the new exponent, so an exponent of one half becomes three halves with a divisor of three halves, giving two thirds of u to the three halves, not u cubed over 3. The correct value is two thirds of the quantity 10 to the three halves minus 1, which is two thirds of the quantity 10 of the square root of 10 minus 1, that is 20.415184. The magnitude of the slip is a useful warning: 333 is sixteen times the right answer, so a result that dwarfs a rough bound on the integrand is a signal that the power rule was botched.
questions.hint: Write the exponent as one half, add one to get three halves, and divide by three halves, which is the same as multiplying by two thirds.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a reliable definite integral evaluation
questions.stem: Put these five actions in the order that evaluates a definite integral correctly, with no step wasted and no error left undetected.

options.text: Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper limit of integration
Locate any discontinuity of the integrand inside the interval and split the integral there
Verify the antiderivative by differentiating it back to the integrand
Subtract the value at the lower limit from the value at the upper limit
Find an antiderivative of the integrand on the whole interval

questions.explanation: The poles come first, because an antiderivative may simply not exist across a discontinuity, so any search for one has to be scoped to an interval where the integrand is continuous. Once that is settled, the antiderivative is found, and differentiating it back is the cheapest available insurance against a botched power rule or a dropped constant. Only then are the two boundary values computed, and the final subtraction is written in the one order that is correct: the value at the upper limit minus the value at the lower limit. The ordering matters most at the two ends. Searching for poles after committing to a single antiderivative risks integrating straight through a singularity, and reversing the subtraction flips the sign of the whole answer, which is the single most common way a correct piece of work ends up reported as a wrong number.
questions.hint: Scope comes before you solve, and verification comes before you evaluate; the subtraction goes upper limit last.
